To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
waist circumference is a better measure of obesity than body mass index for the risk of type 1 diabetes, and that waist circumference is an independent risk factor for type 1 diabetes.

1) the risk of type 1 diabetes was higher among children with higher BMI, 2) the risk of developing type 1 diabetes among obese children was 2.6 times greater than the risk among children with normal weight, and 3) obese children with a BMI above the 97th percentile were 4.4 times more likely to develop diabetes than children with a BMI below the 50th percentile.
waist circumference is a better marker of risk of type 1 diabetes than BMI and that the risk of developing type 1 diabetes is higher in women than men.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of obesity in the development of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
the development of mathematical models and computational algorithms for solving inverse problems, and the application of such models and algorithms for data analysis and decision support.
the development of methods for the statistical analysis of longitudinal data, with a particular focus on the analysis of data from longitudinal cohort studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
waist circumference is a better indicator of risk of type 1 diabetes than body mass index.
obesity is a strong risk factor for type 2 diabetes and that waist circumference is a strong independent risk factor for type-2 diabetes, even in the context of normal weight.
obesity, especially central obesity, is associated with an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the association of obesity and risk of diabetes is not only driven by the association between body mass index (a measure of overall obesity) and diabetes risk but also by the association between measures of regional obesity and diabetes risk.
the association of BMI with diabetes is stronger in younger women and weaker in older women, whereas waist circumference is associated similarly in all age groups.
obesity, particularly abdominal obesity, is associated with an increased risk of diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the association between waist circumference and type 2 diabetes is not explained by body mass index.
it is important to measure waist circumference, as this provides an additional piece of information to the body mass index.
the risk of type  2 diabetes is associated with overall and regional adiposity, and that waist circumference is a better predictor than hip circumference.
